title: The marketplace and moving the skills

story: Monday, 09:10. A teammate improves verify, the shared skill that people and agents use before they say a change is done. From now on it says: in the frontend, start with npm run verify. It is a good idea, but that script does not exist yet; another project adds it to frontend/package.json next month. One reviewer approves the pull request, and at 09:20 it is merged into main of our plugin repository.

By lunch, every laptop that refreshed the plugin has the new text, and so has Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, on every fresh machine it starts. All of them run npm run verify and get "Missing script: verify". Everyone hit the same wall in the same hour, and nobody could see from their own screen which copy of the skill they were running.
hook.question: How do we let a change to a shared skill prove itself on a few machines first, and know exactly which machines have it?

read.h: A marketplace is read at a ref
p: You met the marketplace in an earlier lesson: a git repository with a catalog file, .claude-plugin/marketplace.json, that lists plugins. When a person adds a marketplace, Claude Code clones that repository onto their machine and reads the catalog from it. The question is which commit it reads. Unless you say otherwise, it reads the repository's default branch, main. That is the Monday problem: every merge into main is, a few hours later, on every machine.

Git has a word for "a name that points at a commit": a ref. A branch is a ref that moves when you add commits to it, and a tag is a ref that stays where you put it. Claude Code lets you add a marketplace at a ref by writing it after a # sign, so RhinoHealth/claude-plugins#stable means "our catalog, as it is on the stable branch". The ref a group of people reads is called a release channel, the same idea as Chrome's Stable and Beta: same product, different speed. The comparison stops at one point: Chrome ships a new program, while here a channel is only a branch name, so moving the branch is the release.

code.file: two ways to add the same marketplace
code.text:
# reads main: every merge is live for you after the next refresh
claude plugin marketplace add RhinoHealth/claude-plugins

# reads the stable branch: you get only what someone promoted there
claude plugin marketplace add RhinoHealth/claude-plugins#stable

# a refresh follows the branch you chose, not main
claude plugin marketplace update rhino

notes.text: The part after # is the ref. owner/repo@stable works too.
rhino is the catalog's own name, from the name field in marketplace.json, not the repository's name.

p: We use two branches of one repository. main is the latest channel: every merged pull request lands there, and a few pilot users read it, so a broken change hurts a handful of people who expect it. stable is what everyone else and every agent reads. Once a change has been on main for a week and the nightly evals (the test runs that score each skill) stayed green, someone promotes it. To promote here means to move stable forward to main's commit.

We promote by fast-forward only, which means stable moves to exactly the commit main has, without any commit of its own. The command is a plain push. A fast-forward matters because it makes stable byte for byte what the pilots ran for a week. If people cherry-picked single commits onto stable instead, stable would hold a combination nobody ever tested.
On Monday this would have stayed small: the verify change would have broken the pilots' afternoon, they would have reported it, and stable would never have received it.

code.text:
git fetch origin
git log --oneline origin/stable..origin/main   # what everyone is about to get
git push origin origin/main:stable              # refused if stable has commits main lacks

notes.text: The commits on main that stable does not have yet. Read them before you promote.
A normal push only moves a branch forward. If stable had its own commit, git would refuse, which is what we want.

deeper.h: Go deeper: why the latest channel has its own catalog name
p: A machine can register only one marketplace per name, and our managed settings (the company-wide settings nobody can override on their laptop) register the name rhino at stable for everyone. So the pilots' channel cannot also be called rhino. The repository holds a second catalog file, channels/latest/.claude-plugin/marketplace.json, named rhino-latest, whose entries fetch each plugin from the same repository at ref main.

claude plugin marketplace add has no option for a catalog that is not at the default path, so the latest channel is registered through settings instead, with path set on the source. Pilots get a settings profile that swaps rhino-latest in for rhino. A pilot never has both, because both would offer a plugin called rhino-core.

Moving the branch is not enough to reach a machine. Each laptop keeps an installed copy of every plugin in a cache folder, and Claude Code loads skills from that copy. When it refreshes, it computes the plugin's version: the version field in the plugin's own plugin.json first, then a version in the catalog entry, and only if neither exists, the commit. It replaces the cached copy only when that computed version is different from the one it has.

So a change without a version bump never arrives, however many times you promote it. Worse, a machine that installs the plugin for the first time does get the new files, under the same number. In the lab you will see two laptops that both say 0.2.0 and run different text, which is the Monday problem again: nobody can tell from the number what they run.

That is why plugin CI fails any pull request that changes a plugin without raising its version, and why the version lives in plugin.json only. If the catalog entry also sets one, plugin.json wins without a word, and claude plugin validate warns about the mismatch.

code.file: a laptop on stable, after a promote with no version bump
code.text:
claude plugin marketplace update lab
claude plugin update team-notes@lab

read.see:
✔ Successfully updated marketplace: lab
Checking for updates for plugin "team-notes@lab"…
✔ team-notes is already at the latest version (0.2.0).

read.h: Plugins from other repositories are pinned
p: Two of our plugins do not live in the plugin repository. kb, the plugin that searches the R&D brain (our reviewed pages about our systems), lives with the brain's tools, and fcp-lab, which boots the product on one machine, lives in its own repository. The catalog can still list them. A git-subdir source fetches one folder of another git repository, and a sha (the 40-character id of one commit) pins it to exactly that commit.

A pin means a change in the other repository reaches nobody until someone opens a pull request here that changes the sha. That pull request passes the same CI, gets the same one approval and travels the same channels as everything else. Without the pin, the brain team's next merge would go straight to every laptop, skipping all of it.

notes.text: Fetch one folder of another repository, not the whole repository.
The folder inside that repository that holds the plugin.
The exact commit. A ref alone would follow that repository's branch.

deeper.h: Go deeper: moving the guild skills out of fcp
p: Before the plugin repository existed, the frontend and backend guilds kept their skills in folders inside fcp, our product repository. Those reach only people who open fcp, nothing tests them, and an agent's copy can drift from a person's copy. So the shared ones move into the fe-guild and be-guild plugins, and every reference between them changes to the plugin's namespace, such as be-guild:be-module-cloud, because a plugin's skills are always called plugin-name:skill-name.

A few skills only make sense inside fcp, because they run fcp's own scripts, such as the one that creates test data. They stay in fcp/.claude/skills. Then fcp's committed .claude/settings.json registers the marketplace at stable and enables the two guild plugins, so anyone who opens fcp and accepts the folder trust prompt gets them without typing an install command.

lab.title: Two laptops, two channels, one version
needs: No model calls and no login: plugin commands only
lab.goal: Host a plugin repository on your laptop, read it from two pretend laptops on two channels, promote a change, and see what a missing version bump does.

guess.q: A laptop reads the marketplace at #stable and has team-notes 0.1.0. Someone merges team-notes 0.2.0 into main. The laptop refreshes. What does it run?

options.text: 0.2.0, because a refresh always fetches the newest commit of the repository.
options.why: A refresh fetches the newest commit of the ref the laptop chose. stable has not moved, so its catalog still describes 0.1.0.

options.text: 0.1.0, until someone moves stable to a commit that has 0.2.0.
options.why: The laptop follows its channel. The new version is on main only, so stable readers do not see it yet.

options.text: Nothing: the plugin stops loading because main and stable disagree.
options.why: Two branches that disagree is the normal state of two channels. Each laptop simply reads its own.

follow.say: Make the plugin repository, with one plugin at 0.1.0, and a bare copy that will play the part of GitHub. Push main and stable to it.
follow.do:
mkdir -p ~/academy-labs/g8-1/served && cd ~/academy-labs/g8-1
mkdir -p claude-plugins/.claude-plugin claude-plugins/plugins/team-notes/.claude-plugin claude-plugins/plugins/team-notes/skills/welcome-note
cd claude-plugins && git init -q -b main
cat > .claude-plugin/marketplace.json <<'EOF'
{
  "name": "lab",
  "description": "Plugins for the academy lab",
  "owner": { "name": "Lab" },
  "metadata": { "pluginRoot": "./plugins" },
  "plugins": [
    { "name": "team-notes", "source": "team-notes", "description": "Short notes for the team" }
  ]
}
EOF
cat > plugins/team-notes/.claude-plugin/plugin.json <<'EOF'
{ "name": "team-notes", "version": "0.1.0", "description": "Short notes for the team", "author": { "name": "Lab" } }
EOF
cat > plugins/team-notes/skills/welcome-note/SKILL.md <<'EOF'
---
name: welcome-note
description: "Writes a two-line welcome for a new teammate: hello by first name, the team, and one tip for day one."
---
# welcome-note

Write two lines: hello by first name and the team, then one tip for day one: ask questions in #help.
EOF
git add -A && git commit -qm "team-notes 0.1.0"
git init -q --bare ../served/claude-plugins.git && git remote add origin ../served/claude-plugins.git
git push -q origin main main:stable && claude plugin validate . --strict

follow.say: Claude Code clones a git marketplace over HTTP, the way it would from GitHub, so serve the bare repository with a tiny git server. Run it in a second terminal and leave it open.

Back in the first terminal (the server keeps running in the second), make two pretend laptops. Each one is just a separate Claude Code config folder, so nothing touches your real plugins. The everyone laptop reads stable.
follow.see:
✔ Successfully added marketplace: lab (declared in user settings)
Installing plugin "team-notes@lab"...✔ Successfully installed plugin: team-notes@lab (scope: user)
    Version: 0.1.0

follow.say: Release 0.2.0 on main only, the way a merged pull request would, and refresh the everyone laptop. It should not move, because stable did not.
follow.do:
sed -i '' 's/ask questions in #help/your setup buddy waits in #fe-help/' plugins/team-notes/skills/welcome-note/SKILL.md
sed -i '' 's/"0.1.0"/"0.2.0"/' plugins/team-notes/.claude-plugin/plugin.json
git commit -qam "welcome-note: point new people to their setup buddy (0.2.0)" && git push -q origin main
everyone plugin marketplace update lab && everyone plugin update team-notes@lab
follow.see:
✔ Successfully updated marketplace: lab
Checking for updates for plugin "team-notes@lab"…
✔ team-notes is already at the latest version (0.1.0).

follow.say: A pilot reads main, so the same change reaches them at once. That is the point of the latest channel.
follow.do:
pilot plugin marketplace add "http://localhost:8765/claude-plugins.git#main"
pilot plugin install team-notes@lab
pilot plugin list | grep Version
follow.see:
✔ Successfully added marketplace: lab (declared in user settings)
Installing plugin "team-notes@lab"...✔ Successfully installed plugin: team-notes@lab (scope: user)
    Version: 0.2.0

follow.say: The pilots were happy, so promote: move stable to main's commit with a plain push, then refresh the everyone laptop.
follow.do:
git push -q origin main:stable
everyone plugin marketplace update lab && everyone plugin update team-notes@lab
follow.see:
✔ Successfully updated marketplace: lab
Checking for updates for plugin "team-notes@lab"…
✔ Plugin "team-notes" updated from 0.1.0 to 0.2.0 for scope user. Restart to apply changes.

follow.say: Now the Monday mistake in small: change the skill, forget the version, promote it anyway. Then compare what the everyone laptop really loads (its cache) with the catalog it just fetched.
follow.do:
sed -i '' 's/waits in #fe-help/waits in #fe-help, and lunch is on us/' plugins/team-notes/skills/welcome-note/SKILL.md
git commit -qam "welcome-note: mention lunch" && git push -q origin main main:stable
everyone plugin marketplace update lab && everyone plugin update team-notes@lab
grep -c lunch ../.laptop-everyone/plugins/marketplaces/lab/plugins/team-notes/skills/welcome-note/SKILL.md
grep -c lunch ../.laptop-everyone/plugins/cache/lab/team-notes/0.2.0/skills/welcome-note/SKILL.md
follow.see:
✔ Successfully updated marketplace: lab
✔ team-notes is already at the latest version (0.2.0).
1
0
(the catalog has the lunch line; the copy that Claude loads does not)

lab.build: Pin a plugin that lives in another repository. In ~/academy-labs/g8-1, make a repository kb-tooling with a plugin in its plugin/ folder (plugin.json with name kb and version 1.0.0, and one small skill), commit it, and push it to a bare repo served/kb-tooling.git. Add an entry to the lab catalog with a git-subdir source: url http://localhost:8765/kb-tooling.git, path plugin, and sha set to the commit from git rev-parse HEAD. Push the catalog to main and stable and install kb@lab on the everyone laptop. Then release kb 1.1.0 in kb-tooling and push it: everyone plugin update kb@lab must still say 1.0.0. Finally change the sha in the catalog (your "pull request"), push main and stable, and update again: now it moves to 1.1.0.
checks: The everyone laptop stayed on 0.1.0 while main had 0.2.0, and moved only after git push origin main:stable.
The pilot laptop got 0.2.0 straight from main.
After the promote with no version bump, update said already at the latest version (0.2.0), and grep found the lunch line in the catalog but not in the cache.
kb@lab stayed at 1.0.0 after kb-tooling released 1.1.0, and moved to 1.1.0 only after you changed the sha in the catalog.
claude plugin validate . --strict passes on the catalog with the kb entry.

solution.text:
cd ~/academy-labs/g8-1 && mkdir -p kb-tooling/plugin/.claude-plugin kb-tooling/plugin/skills/kb-search && cd kb-tooling && git init -q -b main
echo '{ "name": "kb", "version": "1.0.0", "description": "Search the team notes", "author": { "name": "Lab" } }' > plugin/.claude-plugin/plugin.json
printf -- '---\nname: kb-search\ndescription: "Searches the team notes and links the page it used."\n---\n# kb-search\n\nSearch the notes first and link the page.\n' > plugin/skills/kb-search/SKILL.md
git add -A && git commit -qm "kb 1.0.0" && git init -q --bare ../served/kb-tooling.git && git remote add origin ../served/kb-tooling.git && git push -q origin main
SHA=$(git rev-parse HEAD)

# in claude-plugins: add this object to "plugins" in .claude-plugin/marketplace.json
#   { "name": "kb", "description": "Search the team notes",
#     "source": { "source": "git-subdir", "url": "http://localhost:8765/kb-tooling.git", "path": "plugin", "sha": "<$SHA>" } }
cd ../claude-plugins && claude plugin validate . --strict && git commit -qam "catalog: add kb" && git push -q origin main main:stable
everyone plugin marketplace update lab && everyone plugin install kb@lab          # Version: 1.0.0

# release kb 1.1.0 in kb-tooling, push it: everyone plugin update kb@lab -> already at 1.0.0
# replace the sha in the catalog, commit, push main and stable: update -> updated from 1.0.0 to 1.1.0

lab.fix: A teammate wanted the catalog to show versions, so they added "version": "0.3.0" to the team-notes entry in marketplace.json and left plugin.json at 0.2.0. Make the same change and run claude plugin validate . --strict: it fails with Entry declares version "0.3.0" but plugins/team-notes/.claude-plugin/plugin.json says "0.2.0". At install time, plugin.json wins … the entry version is silently ignored. Explain what laptops would have installed, then fix the catalog so the version lives in one place only.
explain: Why did the everyone laptop stay on 0.1.0 after main had 0.2.0, and what single command released it?
After the lunch change, two laptops could both say 0.2.0 and run different text. How, and which CI check stops it?
Why is kb pinned by a sha instead of following its own repository's main branch?
lab.done: You promoted a change from main to stable, saw the version gate hold back a change without a bump, pinned an outside plugin by sha, and stopped the git server with Ctrl+C.

check.q: A teammate merges a fix to rhino-core and raises its version from 0.4.0 to 0.4.1. Most laptops read the marketplace at #stable. When do they get the fix?

options.text: At their next session start, because the merge is on the repository's main branch
options.why: Those laptops do not read main. They read stable, and stable still points at the old commit.

options.text: After someone moves stable to a commit that contains the fix, and the laptops refresh
options.why: The ref they chose decides what they see, and the new version decides whether their cached copy is replaced. Both must change.

options.text: Never, unless each person uninstalls and installs rhino-core again
options.why: A refresh with a higher version replaces the cached copy on its own. Reinstalling is not needed.

check.q: Someone promotes a change to a skill but forgot to raise the plugin's version. What do people run afterwards?

options.text: Laptops that already had that version keep the old text; a laptop that installs for the first time gets the new text under the same number
options.why: A cached copy is replaced only when the computed version changes. A fresh install has no cache, so it takes the files as they are now.

options.text: Everyone gets the new text, because stable moved
options.why: Moving the branch changes the catalog each laptop reads, but the version is unchanged, so no cached copy is replaced.

options.text: Nobody gets it, because claude plugin validate refuses to load a skill whose content changed
options.why: validate checks the shape of the files on disk. It does not compare a plugin with the base branch; our own CI script does that.

check.q: Why does our catalog pin the kb plugin, which lives in another repository, to one commit sha?

options.text: Because a git-subdir source cannot follow a branch
options.why: It can: ref names a branch. Following one would be the problem, not a limit.

options.text: Because a sha makes the plugin install faster
options.why: Speed is about the same. The pin is about who decides when a change ships.

options.text: So a change to kb reaches people only through a reviewed pull request in the plugin repository, with its CI and its channels
options.why: Without the pin, the next merge in the other repository would reach every laptop with no review here.

p: Our marketplace is the private repository RhinoHealth/claude-plugins, whose catalog is called rhino. It holds four plugins of our own (rhino-core for every engineer, and fe-guild, be-guild and devops-guild), and lists kb from rnd-kb-tooling and fcp-lab from fcp-local-lab by pinned sha. main is the latest channel, published as a second catalog, channels/latest/.claude-plugin/marketplace.json, named rhino-latest; stable is what everyone and every agent reads. A change is promoted by fast-forwarding stable after a week on latest with green nightly evals. The repository has fcp's ruleset (a pull request and exactly one approval, no bypass for agent apps) and no CODEOWNERS.

Owners live in catalog.yaml instead: every shared skill names its plugin and its owner, who keeps the skill's evals green and runs its monthly rule diet. STYLE.md beside it sets how skills are written. fcp's guild skills move from agents/fe-guild and agents/be-guild into the guild plugins; fcp-only skills such as create-test-data stay in fcp/.claude/skills, and fcp's .claude/settings.json registers rhino at stable and enables fe-guild and be-guild.

tickets.why: The repository, the rhino catalog, the stable and latest channels, versions in plugin.json only, and pinned outside plugins.
Moving fcp's FE and BE skills into the guild plugins, the namespace fixes, and fcp's project settings.
STYLE.md, catalog.yaml with an owner for every skill, and the monthly rule diet.

words.plain: A git name that points at a commit: a branch (it moves) or a tag (it stays).
The ref a group of people reads the marketplace at: stable for everyone, main for pilots.
Move stable forward to main's commit with a fast-forward push, after the change proved itself on main.
The version Claude Code works out for a plugin, from plugin.json first; a cached copy is replaced only when it changes.
Point a catalog entry at one exact commit of another repository, so only a pull request here can change it.

review.q: Draw the path of one skill change from a merged pull request to every laptop, naming the two things that must change for a laptop to get it.
review.a: Merge to main (pilots on the latest channel get it if the version was raised), a week with green nightly evals, a fast-forward push of stable, then each laptop refreshes. The ref they read must point at the new commit, and the computed version must be different.

review.q: A teammate says "just let everyone read main, it is simpler". What do you answer?
review.a: Then every merge reaches every person and every agent within hours, with nobody testing it first, which is the Monday problem. Two channels cost one branch and one push per release.

review.q: Two people both see verify at 0.6.0 but get different instructions. What happened, and what prevents it?
review.a: A change was promoted without a version bump: the older install kept its cached copy and the newer install took the new files under the same number. Plugin CI fails a pull request that changes a plugin without raising its version.

remember: A laptop gets a change when the ref it reads moves and the plugin's version changes, so promote stable on purpose and raise the version on every change.
